Anyon Condensation: Coherent states, Symmetry Enriched Topological Phases, Goldstone Theorem, and Dynamical Rearrangement of Symmetry
Yuting Hu, Zichang Huang, Ling-yan Hung, Yidun Wan

Abstract
Although the mathematics of anyon condensation in topological phases has been studied intensively in recent years, a proof of its physical existence is tantamount to constructing an effective Hamiltonian theory. In this paper, we concretely establish the physical foundation of anyon condensation by building the effective Hamiltonian and the Hilbert space, in which we explicitly construct the vacuum of the condensed phase as the coherent states that are the eigenstates of the creation operators that create the condensate anyons. Along with this construction, which is analogous to Laughlin’s construction of wavefunctions of fractional quantum hall states, we generalize the Goldstone theorem in the usual spontaneous symmetry breaking paradigm to the case of anyon condensation. We then prove that the condensed phase is a symmetry enriched (protected) topological phase by directly constructing the corresponding symmetry transformations, which can be considered as a generalization of the Bogoliubov transformation.



1
Introduction

Anyon condensation has a ubiquitous presence in the study of topological order, particularly in 2+1 dimensions . It characterizes topological boundary conditions and defects between phases
Bais and Slingerland 2009
;
Kitaev and Kong 2012
;
Barkeshli et al. 2013a
;
Barkeshli et al. 2013b
;
Hung and Wan 2015a
;
Hung and Wan 2015b
;
Cong et al. 2017
;
Wan and Wang 2017
. It also provides mathematical maps (functors) between phases, giving new insights to the mathematical structures of, and relations between topological orders. Notably, the parent phase—the phase before anyon condensation—and its child phase—the condensed phase—also encapsulate data of a symmetry enriched topological (SET)
Maciejko et al. 2010
;
Swingle et al. 2011
;
Levin and Stern 2012
;
Mesaros and Ran 2013
;
Hung and Wan 2014
;
Barkeshli et al. 2019
;
Gu et al. 2014
or a symmetry protected topological (SPT) phase
Affleck et al. 1987
;
Chen et al. 2011
. The mathematical framework describing anyon condensation has been provided in
Kitaev and Kong 2012
;
Kong 2014
. Yet the concept is often regarded as being mysterious particularly to physicists, since the mathematical description based on Frobenius algebra
A
(describing the condensate) in a modular tensor category
\mathcal{C}
and its representation (describing excitations in the condensate) do not appear to be directly related to states in a Hilbert space—a fundamental physical ingredient that would convince a physicist that the phenomenon exists. An explicit construction in the current context is comparable to the construction of the Laughlin wave-function that illustrates the existence of the fractional quantum hall state
Laughlin 1983
. The wave-function also lays out the possibility, if not a concrete path, towards realizing or simulating it in an experiment.

Moreover, the notion of ‘condensation’ would be immediately associated with spontaneous symmetry breaking in a physicist’s mind. The analogy has been invoked in many discussions of anyon condensation. Nevertheless, if the analogy is more than just an analogy, it would be necessary to understand in what sense the new ground state is a coherent state of the condensate, and that one would expect that the Goldstone theorem to have a counterpart in these topological condensates.

In this paper, we would like to address these questions. Along the way, our techniques will also find applications in understanding the symmetry enriched/protected topological (SET/SPT) phases through the lens of anyon condensation, allowing us to systematically construct symmetry action on explicit states in the Hilbert space of the child phase, completing the program instigated in
Hung and Wan 2013
;
Hung and Wan 2014
;
Gu et al. 2014
.

The key results of this paper are:

1.

We build the explicit Hilbert space and construct creation operators that create the condensate anyons. Then we explicitly construct the vacua of the condensed phase as the coherent states that are eigenvectors of the creation operators that create condensate anyons.

2.

We classify the inequivalent ground states that emerge for a given condensate in a twisted quantum double model (Dijkgraaf-Witten discrete gauge theory) based on the Tannaka duality. This is a generalization of the Goldstone theorem in the context of anyon condensation in topological orders, where the condensate could be magnetic/dyonic excitations with respect to the gauge group, unlike in the usual context in which the Goldstone theorem or the Higgs mechanism applies, the condensate are purely electric excitations.

3.

We prove by construction that the condensed phase is a symmetry enriched (protected) topological phase, where the symmetry is a hidden global symmetry, described by a finite group
G
, and construct the corresponding symmetry transformations. The group
G
is constructed from
A
using Tannaka reconstruction theorem. Hence, there are
|G|
sectors respectively labeled by the
G
elements. The condensed phase lives in one sector—the physical sector.

4.

The global
G
transformation is decomposed into two actions: one mixes the anyons of the same energy within one sector and is characterized by a
G
-action on
\mathrm{Rep}A
, while the other maps one sector to another. This is a generalization of the Bogoliubov transformation for coherent states in the context of anyon condensation.

We shall briefly explain these key result in Section
2
before we derive them in details. We supply explicit examples to the results above. In the case of charge condensation and the case of dyon condensation in twisted quantum double models of arbitrary gauge group
G
we supply a complete solution to the above construction.

If certain anyons in
\mathcal{U}
are in a more general representations
\rho^{\prime}
, they are organized into doublets or multiplets of
G
, that is, these anyons can be exchanged or permuted. When a physical boundary exists, an SET phase has stable gapless edge modes protected by the global symmetry.

This paper is organized as follows. Section
2
briefly explains our key results by exposing the relevant physics rather than mathematical details and presents a dictionary between the concepts in superconductor and their counterparts in anyon condensation. Section
3
further aids the brief exposition by two simple examples, namely the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
toric code and doubled semion models. Section
4.1
explicitly constructs the coherent states that describe the condensates of anyons in the most generic setting. Section
4.2
constructs the symmetry transformation in condensed phases. With the doubled Ising topological phase, Section
4.3
exemplifies that anyon condensation leads to a child phase being an SET phase. Section
5
(
6
) solves in the TQD model the problem of charge (dyon) condensation that leads to a group symmetry. Section
7
discusses the reverse process of anyon condensation, i.e., gauging an SET/SPT phase to a topological phase without a global symmetry. The appendices collect certain calculations too detailed to be part of the main text.

We shall also show that there is a hidden global symmetry in the condensed phase and construct the corresponding symmetry transformations. This symmetry renders the condensed phase an SET or SPT phase.

Suppose

is the representation category of some quantum group
2

2

More precisely, we mean quasi Hopf algebras or more generally weak Hopf algebras.

Q

, or in other words, the

-symmetry is hidden from the physical Hilbert space.

To see this, we add to

(3)

where

prefers particular ground states that do not manifest the

-symmetry. In the end of the day, we should take

.

To make precise the above mechanism, we focus on a special case where the spontaneously broken symmetry is a finite group
G
. This happens if

,

3
3

3

Mathematically, this extension is equivalent to construct a fibre functor

.

U_{g}
to act on all anyons in the condensed phase. We show that

(i)

[H_{0},U_{g}]=0
.

(ii)

The Hilbert space are divided into
|G|
sectors. This collection of states can be understood as a discrete zero mode of a generalized Goldstone mode.
The chosen

does not commute with

and hence selects a particular sector as the physical one.

With this global
G
-symmetry, the resulting condensed phase is a symmetry enriched (protected) topological phase.

We emphasize the distinction between ‘symmetry’ and ‘invariance’. The original
Q
-invariance of the Hamiltonian is never lost. The above construction implies that a
G
-sub-symmetry is hidden in the condensed phase. The survived symmetry is encoded in the topological observables characterized by
\mathrm{Rep}A
.

We call such a change of the manifestation of symmetry a

. Concretely, the

-invariance is rearranged as

(i)

The surviving symmetry encoded by topological observables characterized by
\mathrm{Rep}A
.

(ii)

The hidden global symmetry transformation

is decomposed into two parts(See Fig.

(a)

The mixing of anyons with the same energy within one sector.

(b)

When expressed in terms of coherent states, each sector is labeled by coherent parameters
\{g_{n}\}
. The

maps one sector to another by
\{g_{n}\}\mapsto\{gg_{n}\}
.

Figure 2:

\{gg_{n}\}

Mathematically, the decomposition of the global transformation

is characterized by the
equivariantization category

(\mathrm{Rep}A)^{G}
whose objects are
(V,u_{g})
for

and

is an equivariant structure. The mapping from one sector to another under
U_{g}
can be formulated by

where

is a group action on
\mathrm{Rep}A
. The mixing of anyons with the same energy within each sector can be formulated by the equivariant structure
u_{g}:T_{g}(V)\to V
. The equivalence
(\mathrm{Rep}A)^{G}\cong\mathcal{C}
implies that the
Q
-invariance can be recovered from the hidden global
G
-symmetry.

As concrete examples of the above mechanism, we explicitly construct the effective theory of the charge condensation in the twisted quantum double models, leading to SPT phases.

3
Condensed states: in toric code model and double semion model

In this section we study the bosonic anyon condensation in the toric code model and double semion model as two simplest examples to demonstrate our results. We will construct the coherent states and show the dynamical symmetry rearrangement.

3.1
Example: in toric Code Model

In the toric code model, elementary excitations carry topological charges: vacuum
\mathbf{1}
,
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
charge
e
,
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
flux
m
, and the charge-flux composite
em
. Let us condense
e
. After the condensation, two topological charges remains:
A=\mathbf{1}\oplus e
and
B=m\oplus em
.

In what follows we consider charge condensation, so
A=1\oplus e
, where
e
is the charge excitation in the toric code model. The new vacuum, i.e., the vacuum of the condensed phase, will be the superposition of states of arbitrary many
e
’s.

We start with the basis vectors

|a;j_{1},j_{2},\dotsc,j_{N}\rangle,

(4)

where
a\in\{1,e\}
, and
j_{n}\in\{1,e,m,em\}
the topological charge of the
n
-th anyon (Fig.
1
). Note that the degeneracy label
\mu
in Eq. (
1
) does not exist here.

By using the basis (
4
), we assume the total topological charge could be either
1
or
e
. We may have other types of constraints on the total topological charge depending on the boundary conditions of the system. Nevertheless, such constraints will not affect our results derived in this paper. Thus, for simplicity, we do not specify boundary conditions in the rest of the paper.

3.1.1
Creation Operator and coherent states

In this example, define the
creation operator

W_{n}(e)
by

W_{n}(e)|a;j_{1},j_{2},\dotsc,j_{n},\dots,j_{N}\rangle=|e\otimes a;j_{1},j_{2},\dotsc,e\otimes j_{n},\dots,j_{N}\rangle,

(5)

with
n=1,\dots,N-1
, which creates a pair of
e
in the condensate and fuse one of them to
j_{n}
.

In the following, we will construct the simultaneous eigenvectors of
W_{n}(e)
. We will use them to construct the condensed states later.
Since
W^{2}_{n}(e)=1
,
W_{n}(e)
has eigenvalues
\pm 1
.

We first consider the case with positive eigenvalues:
W_{n}(e)|\Phi\rangle=|\Phi\rangle

\forall n
. The eigenspace
\mathcal{H}^{W=1}
, i.e., the physical Hilbert space, has basis vectors

|A;V_{1},V_{2},\dotsc,V_{N}\rangle,

(6)

which abbreviates
\left|{A}\right\rangle\otimes\left|{V_{1}}\right\rangle\otimes\dots\otimes\left|{V_{N}}\right\rangle
, where
V_{n}=A,B
, with
\left|{A}\right\rangle=\frac{\left|{1}\right\rangle+\left|{e}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}
, and
B=\frac{\left|{m}\right\rangle+\left|{em}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}
. Note that we only allow the basis states with even occurrences of
B
. For example, the state
|A;A,B,\dotsc,B\rangle
is expanded as

|A;A,B,\dotsc,B\rangle=2^{-(N+1)/2}\sum_{a=1,e}\sum_{j_{1}=1,e}\sum_{j_{2}=m,em}\dotsc\sum_{j_{N}=m,em}|a;j_{1},j_{2},\dotsc,j_{N}\rangle,

(7)

in terms of the basis vectors (
4
).

The basis vectors (
6
) span the physical Hilbert space of the condensed phase, where
\left|{A;A,A,\dots,A}\right\rangle
is the vacuum that is the superposition of arbitrary many condensate anyons.

Now define a
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
operator
u_{-}
by

\displaystyle u_{-}\left|{1}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\left|{1}\right\rangle,

(8)

\displaystyle u_{-}\left|{e}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=-\left|{e}\right\rangle,

\displaystyle u_{-}\left|{m}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\left|{m}\right\rangle,

\displaystyle u_{-}\left|{em}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=-\left|{em}\right\rangle.

Let
u_{+}=\mathrm{id}
, such that
\{u_{g},g=\pm\}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{2}=
under multiplication. We also define

\left|{V^{g}}\right\rangle:=u_{g}\left|{V}\right\rangle,

(9)

for
V=A,B
. All simultaneous eigenvectors of
W_{n}(e)
are generated from
|A;V_{1},V_{2},\dotsc,V_{N}\rangle
by
u_{g}
:

\begin{aligned} &W_{n}(e)|A^{g_{0}};V_{1}^{g_{1}},V_{2}^{g_{2}},\dotsc,V_{n}^{g_{n}},\dotsc,V_{N}^{g_{N}}\rangle\\
=\,&(g_{0}g_{n})|A^{g_{0}};V_{1}^{g_{1}},V_{2}^{g_{2}},\dotsc,V_{n}^{g_{n}},\dotsc,V_{N}^{g_{N}}\rangle\end{aligned}.

(10)

The eigenvalues are computed from the commutator relation

W_{n}u_{g_{0}}u_{g_{n}}=(g_{0}g_{n})u_{g_{0}}u_{g_{n}}W_{n}.

(11)

We call these eigenvectors the
coherent states
of the creation operators
W_{n}(e)
, and call the eigenvalues
\{g_{0};g_{1},g_{2},\dotsc,g_{N}\}
the coherent parameters.

We summarize the orthonormal condition of the coherent states:

\displaystyle\langle A^{g_{0}};V_{1}^{g_{1}},\dotsc,V_{N}^{g_{N}}\left|{A^{g^{\prime}_{0}};{V^{\prime}}_{1}^{g^{\prime}_{1}},\dotsc,{V^{\prime}}_{N}^{g^{\prime}_{N}}}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\,

\displaystyle\delta_{g_{0},g^{\prime}_{0}}\delta_{g_{1},g^{\prime}_{1}}\dots\delta_{g_{N},g^{\prime}_{N}}\delta_{V_{1},V^{\prime}_{1}}\dots\delta_{V_{N},V^{\prime}_{N}}

(12)

3.1.2
Effective Hamiltonian and the global symmetry

We define the effective Hamiltonian as

H_{0}=-\sum_{n}Q_{n}-\sum_{n}W_{n},\quad Q_{n}\left|{j_{n}}\right\rangle=\delta_{j_{n}\in A}\left|{j_{n}}\right\rangle,

(13)

where
\delta_{j_{n}\in A}=1
if
j_{n}\in\{1,e\}
and
0
otherwise.

We shall add to
H_{0}
an extra infinitesimal Hamiltonian

H_{\epsilon}=\epsilon\sum_{n}\Phi_{n},\quad\Phi_{n}\left|{A^{g_{0}};V^{g_{1}}_{1},\dots,V^{g_{N}}_{N}}\right\rangle=\delta_{g_{n},+}\left|{A^{g_{0}};V^{g_{1}}_{1},\dots,V^{g_{N}}_{N}}\right\rangle.

(14)

We should take the limit
\epsilon\to 0
at the end of calculation.

We can construct the global symmetry transformation
U_{g}
by

U_{g}|A^{g_{0}};V_{1}^{g_{1}},\dotsc,V_{N}^{g_{N}}\rangle=|A^{gg_{0}};V_{1}^{gg_{1}},\dotsc,V_{N}^{gg_{N}}\rangle.

(15)

Obviously,
[H_{0},U_{g}]=0
. In the limit
\epsilon\to 0
, there are two ground states

\left|{A^{\pm};A^{\pm},\dots,A^{\pm}}\right\rangle.

(16)

However, due to the presence of
H_{\epsilon}
, the actual ground state is

\left|{A^{+};A^{+},\dots,A^{+}}\right\rangle.

(17)

3.2
Example: in double semion model

The double semion model is identical to the twisted quantum double model defined by
G=\mathbb{Z}_{2}
and a non-trivial 3-cocycle over
G
, we use the same symbols to label the topological charges as in the toric code model. However, there is a difference: these topological charges obey nontrivial braiding statistics:
e
is called the doubled semion,
m
the semion, and
em
the anti-semion.

We condense the doubled semion
e
, using the Frobenius algebra
A=1\oplus e
. The creation operator
W_{n}
is defined as in Eq. (
8
). To construct the coherent states, we define the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
action by

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} u_{-}\left|{1}\right\rangle&=\left|{1}\right\rangle,\\
u_{-}\left|{e}\right\rangle&=-\left|{e}\right\rangle,\\
u_{-}\left|{m}\right\rangle&=\mathrm{i}\left|{m}\right\rangle,\\
u_{-}\left|{em}\right\rangle&=-\mathrm{i}\left|{em}\right\rangle.\end{aligned}

(18)

and set
u_{+}=\mathrm{id}
.

The local
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
action is different from that in the toric code model. When acting on
m
and
em
,
u_{-}
is a projective representation:
u_{-}u_{-}=-u_{+}
.

Define
A^{\pm}=\frac{\left|{1}\right\rangle+\left|{e}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}
and
B^{+}=\frac{\left|{m}\right\rangle+\left|{em}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}
,
B^{-}=\mathrm{i}\frac{\left|{m}\right\rangle-\left|{em}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}
. Now the coherent states has the same form as in the toric code case:

\displaystyle W_{n}(e)|A^{g_{0}};V_{h_{1}}^{g_{1}},V_{h_{2}}^{g_{2}},\dotsc,V_{h_{n}}^{g_{n}},\dotsc,V_{h_{N}}^{g_{N}}\rangle

\displaystyle=\,

\displaystyle(g_{0}g_{n})|A^{g_{0}};V_{h_{1}}^{g_{1}},V_{h_{2}}^{g_{2}},\dotsc,V_{h_{n}}^{g_{n}},\dotsc,V_{h_{N}}^{g_{N}}\rangle,

(19)

where we set
V_{h=+}^{g}=A^{g}
and
V_{h=-}^{g}=B^{g}
, for convenience of future computation.

The global symmetry transformation is given by

\displaystyle U_{g}|A^{g_{0}};V_{h_{1}}^{g_{1}},V_{h_{2}}^{g_{2}},\dotsc,V_{h_{n}}^{g_{n}},\dotsc,V_{h_{N}}^{g_{N}}\rangle

\displaystyle=\,

\displaystyle\mu_{g}(h_{1},h_{2})\mu_{g}(h_{1}h_{2},h_{3})\dots\mu_{g}(h_{1}h_{2}\dots h_{N-1},h_{N})

\displaystyle\beta_{h_{1}}(g,g_{1})\beta_{h_{2}}(g,g_{2})\dots\beta_{h_{N}}(g,g_{N})

\displaystyle\qquad\quad|A^{gg_{0}};V_{h_{1}}^{gg_{1}},V_{h_{2}}^{gg_{2}},\dotsc,V_{h_{n}}^{gg_{n}},\dotsc,V_{h_{N}}^{gg_{N}}\rangle,

(20)

where
\beta_{h_{n}}(g,g_{n})=-1
if
h_{n}=g=g_{n}=-
and 1 otherwise,
\mu_{g}(h_{1},h_{2})=-1
if
g=h_{1}=h_{2}=-
and
1
otherwise.

We shown the charge condensation in the twisted quantum double models with input data
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
. In Section
5
, we will deal with a generic twisted quantum double model.

4
Effective theory of anyon condensation in generic cases

In this section, we will construct an effective theory of anyon condensation in generic cases. We will construct coherent states for the condensed phases in generic cases, and construct the hidden global symmetry transformation.

4.1
Coherent States

We take a topological phase characterized by a modular tensor category
\mathcal{C}
and study an anyon condensation characterized by a strongly separable commutative Frobenius algebra
A\in\mathcal{C}
. Denote by
L_{\mathcal{C}}
the set of all representative simple objects of
\mathcal{C}
, by
L_{A}\subset L_{\mathcal{C}}
the subset of those that are the direct summands in
A
, and by
L_{\mathrm{Rep}A}
the set of all representative simple objects of
\mathrm{Rep}A

They are the basis vectors of
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(a_{0},a_{1}\otimes j_{1}\otimes j_{2}\otimes\dotsc\otimes j_{N})
, where
a_{0},a_{1},a_{2}\in L_{A}
,
j_{1},\dots,j_{N},i_{1},\dots\in L_{\mathcal{C}}
and
L_{\mathcal{C}}
. (For computing with concrete tensors, we fix an appropriate basis of
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(i,j\otimes k)
for all
i,j,k\in L_{\mathcal{C}}
. In the diagram, we have also suppressed the multiplicity degrees of freedom at trivalent vertices.) The above diagram depicts the relevant quantum observables: a topological charge
j_{n}
with the
n
-th quasiparticle, and a total topological charge
i_{n-1}
of the subsystem of first
n
quasiparticles. The total topological charge is
a_{0}
. In a real system, the constraint on the total topological charge depends on the boundary condition. We shall not dwell on such constraints since they will not affect our results.

We consider a special situation, where the
a
-anyons only appears in the ground states. Mathematically, if
A
is
absorbing
, i.e.,
A\otimes A=A^{\oplus n}
for
n\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}
as
A
-modules in
\mathrm{Rep}A
, then a finite group
G
can be constructed
Deligne 2007
;
Müger 2004
according to Tannaka reconstruction theorem. Namely, there exits a unique finite group
G
, such that
A
is identified with the regular representation of
G
.
Rigorously, we define
G
by

(27)

where
V_{1},V_{2},\dots,U_{1},U_{2},\dots\in L_{\mathrm{Rep}A}
. The
g\in G
can be chosen arbitrarily. The diagram is a composition of a morphism in
\mathrm{Hom}_{A}(A,A{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}V_{1}{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}V_{2}{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}\dotsc{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}V_{N})
and a
\mathcal{C}
-morphism
g\in\mathrm{Aut}(A)=G
. In the diagram, we suppress the indices due to the multiplicities in
\mathrm{Hom}_{A}
. The diagram depicts the relevant quantum observables: the topological charge
V_{n}
at the
n
-th quasiparticle, and a total topological charge
U_{n-1}
of the first
n
quasiparticles.

One can verify
[W^{g}_{n},W^{g^{\prime}}_{n^{\prime}}]=0
straightforwardly. Hence, we can define the
coherent states
as the simultaneous eigenvectors of
W^{g}_{n}
for all
n
and
g
. It is convenient to use them as the new basis instead of that in Eq. (
21
).

We now explicitly construct the coherent states, in a way similar to that in the previous subsection: We can generate the coherent states by acting some local operators
u_{g}
on the
W_{n}
-invariant basis (
27
).

A group element
g
is an automorphism of
A
and induces a group structure on any generic object in
\mathrm{Rep}A
. In Appendix
C.2
, we prove that for every
(V,\rho_{V})\in L_{\mathrm{Rep}A}
and
g\in G
, there exits an object
(V,\rho^{\prime}_{V})\in L_{\mathrm{Rep}A}
, and a unique
\mathcal{C}
-isomorphism
u_{g}:V\to V
, such that

(28)

{u_{g}}

(29)

Because the action of
{u_{g}}
is associative,
\beta_{(V,\rho_{V})}
is a 2-cocycle.

u_{g}
on
W_{n}

(30)

where
V_{1},\dots,V_{N},U_{1},\dots\in L_{\mathrm{Rep}A}
,

\displaystyle\alpha_{1}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{A}(U_{1},V^{\prime}_{1}{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}V^{\prime}_{2}),

(31)

\displaystyle\alpha_{2}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{A}(U_{2},U_{1}{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}V^{\prime}_{3}),

\displaystyle\dots

and
u_{\overline{g_{n}}}:V^{\prime}_{n}\to V_{n}
with
\overline{g_{n}}\equiv g_{n}^{-1}
.

The defining property (
28
) implies an eigenvalue equation

\displaystyle W_{n}^{(g_{n}\overline{g_{0}})}\left|{g_{0}A;g_{1}V_{1},g_{2}V_{2},\dots,g_{N}V_{N};U_{1},U_{2},\dots;\alpha}\right\rangle

(32)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left|{g_{0}A;g_{1}V_{1},g_{2}V_{2},\dots,g_{N}V_{N};U_{1},U_{2},\dots;\alpha}\right\rangle.

Hence, we dub the states (
30
) the
coherent states
with the coherent parameters
g_{1},\dots,g_{N}
.

The coherent states form a new basis of the effective Hilbert space. Eq. (
30
) is an orthonormal basis of
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(A,A\otimes V_{1}\otimes V_{2}\otimes\dots\otimes V_{N})
.
To see this, we need only look at the decomposition of
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(U_{1},V_{1}\otimes V_{2})
:

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(U_{1},V_{1}\otimes V_{2})

(33)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hom}_{A}(U_{1},F(V_{1}\otimes V_{2}))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hom}_{A}(U_{1},FV_{1}{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}FV_{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\bigoplus_{g_{1},g_{2}\in G}\mathrm{Hom}_{A}(U_{1},T_{g_{1}}V_{1}{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}T_{g_{2}}V_{2}),

where
F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathrm{Rep}A
is the free functor given in Eq. (
133
), and
h_{1}
can be any group element. The first equality above follows Eq. (
136
), and in the third equality, use is made of the decomposition
FV=\oplus_{g}T_{g}V
as in Proposition
4
(i) of Appendix
C.4
.

Using the creation operator
W_{n}
, we can define the effective Hamiltonian as in Eq. (
2
), and we obtained the a physical Hilbert space spanned by
\left|{gA;gV_{1},gV_{2},\dots,gV_{N};U_{1},U_{2},\dots;\alpha}\right\rangle
, where
g
is randomly chosen by the system.

4.2
Symmetry transformations

u_{g}
acts, we first introduce a grading. Namely, for every simple
(Z,\rho)\in\mathrm{Rep}A

(34)

The grading is conjugated under
u_{g}
:
\mathrm{\mathbf{gr}}u_{g}(Z,\rho)=g\mathrm{\mathbf{gr}}(Z,\rho)\overline{g}
. See Appendix
C.1
for more properties.

We shall use
u_{g}
to study the transformations of the coherent states, so we need to know how to transform
\alpha\in\mathrm{Hom}_{A}((U,\rho_{U}),(V,\rho_{V})\otimes_{A}(W,\rho_{W}))
. Define
{{}^{g}\alpha}

where
a
runs over the summands of
A
and
x_{1},x_{2}
over those of
V
. The six simple objects are listed as

\begin{array}[]{|c|c|}\hline\cr 0\bar{0}\oplus 2\bar{2}&\begin{array}[]{cccc}\rho_{0\bar{0},0\bar{0}}^{0\bar{0}}=1&\rho_{2\bar{2},2\bar{2}}^{0\bar{0}}=1&\rho_{0\bar{0},2\bar{2}}^{2\bar{2}}=\frac{1}{\xi}&\rho_{2\bar{2},0\bar{0}}^{2\bar{2}}=\xi\\
\end{array}\\
\hline\cr 0\bar{2}\oplus 2\bar{0}&\begin{array}[]{cccc}\rho_{0\bar{2},0\bar{2}}^{0\bar{0}}=1&\rho_{2\bar{0},2\bar{0}}^{0\bar{0}}=1&\rho_{0\bar{2},2\bar{0}}^{2\bar{2}}=\frac{1}{\xi}&\rho_{2\bar{0},0\bar{2}}^{2\bar{2}}=\xi\\
\end{array}\\
\hline\cr{1\bar{1}}_{-}&\begin{array}[]{cc}\rho_{1\bar{1},1\bar{1}}^{0\bar{0}}=1&\rho_{1\bar{1},1\bar{1}}^{2\bar{2}}=-1\\
\end{array}\\
\hline\cr{1\bar{1}}_{+}&\begin{array}[]{cc}\rho_{1\bar{1},1\bar{1}}^{0\bar{0}}=1&\rho_{1\bar{1},1\bar{1}}^{2\bar{2}}=1\\
\end{array}\\
\hline\cr 0\bar{1}\oplus 2\bar{1}&\begin{array}[]{cccc}\rho_{0\bar{1},0\bar{1}}^{0\bar{0}}=1&\rho_{2\bar{1},2\bar{1}}^{0\bar{0}}=1&\rho_{0\bar{1},2\bar{1}}^{2\bar{2}}=\frac{1}{\xi}&\rho_{2\bar{1},0\bar{1}}^{2\bar{2}}=\xi\\
\end{array}\\
\hline\cr 1\bar{0}\oplus 1\bar{2}&\begin{array}[]{cccc}\rho_{1\bar{0},1\bar{0}}^{0\bar{0}}=1&\rho_{1\bar{2},1\bar{2}}^{0\bar{0}}=1&\rho_{1\bar{0},1\bar{2}}^{2\bar{2}}=\frac{1}{\xi}&\rho_{1\bar{2},1\bar{0}}^{2\bar{2}}=\xi\\
\end{array}\\
\hline\cr\end{array},

(45)

where
\xi
is a free parameter to choose. We set
\xi=1
in the following. Will use a subscript
\pm
to distinguish the third and the fourth objects who have the same
V=1\bar{1}
.

The group
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
is reconstructed as

G=\mathrm{Aut}A=\{\mathrm{id}_{0\bar{0}}\pm\mathrm{id}_{2\bar{2}}\}.

(46)

For simplicity, we denote the elements by
\pm
.

These six simple objects in
\mathrm{Rep}A
are graded by
G=\mathbb{Z}_{2}=\{+,-\}
. The first four are graded by
g=+
, while the last two by
g=-
.

The group action
T_{g}
maps
{1\bar{1}}_{\pm}\to{1\bar{1}}_{\mp}
, and any other object to itself. The quivariant structure
u_{+}=\mathrm{id}_{V}
and
u_{-}
is given by

\begin{array}[]{|c|c|}\hline\cr 0\bar{0}\oplus 2\bar{2}&u_{-}=\mathrm{id}_{0\bar{0}}-\mathrm{id}_{2\bar{2}}\\
\hline\cr 0\bar{2}\oplus 2\bar{0}&u_{-}=\mathrm{id}_{0\bar{2}}-\mathrm{id}_{2\bar{0}}\\
\hline\cr{1\bar{1}}_{-}&u_{-}=\mathrm{id}_{1\bar{1}}\\
\hline\cr{1\bar{1}}_{+}&u_{-}=\mathrm{id}_{1\bar{1}}\\
\hline\cr 0\bar{1}\oplus 2\bar{1}&u_{-}=\mathrm{id}_{0\bar{1}}-\mathrm{id}_{2\bar{1}}\\
\hline\cr 1\bar{0}\oplus 1\bar{2}&u_{-}=\mathrm{id}_{1\bar{0}}-\mathrm{id}_{1\bar{2}}\\
\hline\cr\end{array}

(47)

As a result, the group action
T:\underline{G}\to\mathrm{Aut}_{\otimes}\mathcal{C}
has the trivial tensor structure
\mathrm{id}_{V}:T_{gh}V\to T_{g}T_{h}V
. The functor
T_{g}
also has the trivial tensor structure
\mathrm{id}_{V{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}W}:T_{g}(V{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}W)\to T_{g}V{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}T_{g}W
.

5
Charge condensation in Twisted quantum double phases

Consider a twisted quantum double phase
Hu et al. 2013
characterized by
\mathcal{C}=\mathrm{Rep}(D^{\omega}G)
, the representation category of the quantum double
D^{\omega}G
, with
G
a finite group and
\omega\in H^{3}[G,U(1)]
. For the definition of
D^{\omega}G
and a brief review of its representations, see Appendix
D
.

Consider a charge condensation, in which all the charges condense. We shall first concretely construct a Frobenius algebra
A\in\mathcal{C}
for such a condensation, and then derive the coherent states and the symmetry transformations
U_{g}
defined previously.

The dual algebra
(D^{\omega}G)^{*}
of
D^{\omega}G
is a representation of
D^{\omega}G
, with the representation matrix given by

\pi^{R}(\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{h})\left|{\mathrm{A}^{g^{\prime}}\mathrm{B}^{h^{\prime}}}\right\rangle=\left|{\mathrm{A}^{g^{\prime}}\mathrm{B}^{h^{\prime}}\mathrm{B}^{h}(\mathrm{A}^{x})^{-1}}\right\rangle=\delta_{h,h^{\prime}}\frac{1}{\beta_{gh\overline{g}}(g,\overline{g})}\left|{\mathrm{A}^{g^{\prime}\overline{g}}\mathrm{B}^{gh^{\prime}\overline{g}}}\right\rangle,

(48)

where
(\mathrm{A}^{x})^{-1}
is defined by
\mathrm{A}^{x}(\mathrm{A}^{x})^{-1}\mathrm{B}^{y}=\mathrm{B}^{y}
for all
y\in G
.

We consider two morphisms of the representations of
D^{\omega}G
: the coproduct
\Delta:(D^{\omega}G)^{*}\to(D^{\omega}G)^{*}\otimes(D^{\omega}G)^{*}

and its transpose
\Delta^{*}:(D^{\omega}G)^{*}\otimes(D^{\omega}G)^{*}\to(D^{\omega}G)^{*}
. The transpose
\Delta^{*}
is defined by

\Delta^{*}:\left|{\mathrm{A}^{g_{1}}\mathrm{B}^{h_{1}}}\right\rangle\otimes\left|{\mathrm{A}^{g_{2}}\mathrm{B}^{h_{2}}}\right\rangle\mapsto\delta_{g_{1},g_{2}}\mu_{g_{1}}(h_{1},h_{2})\left|{\mathrm{A}^{g_{1}}\mathrm{B}^{h_{1}h_{2}}}\right\rangle,

(49)

where
\Delta
is defined in Eq. (
198
) and
\mu
is the coproduct structure defined in Eq. (
204
).

Let

V_{h}=\text{vector space spanned by }\{\mathrm{B}^{h}\mathrm{A}^{g}\}_{g\in G}.

(50)

Obviously,
(V_{h},\pi^{R})
is a representation of
D^{\omega}G
. We shall use them to construct the Frobenius algebra
A
and
\mathrm{Rep}A
.

Let

A=V_{h=1}.

(51)

Then
(A,\Delta^{*})
is an associative algebra. Moreover, it carries a commutative Frobenius algebra structure, given by

\Delta^{*}:A\otimes A\to A,\quad|{\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{1}}\rangle\otimes|{\mathrm{A}^{g^{\prime}}\mathrm{B}^{1}}\rangle\mapsto\delta_{g,g^{\prime}}|{\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{1}}\rangle,

(52)

\Delta:A\to A\otimes A,\quad|{\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{1}}\rangle\mapsto|{\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{1}}\rangle\otimes|{\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{1}}\rangle,

(53)

\epsilon^{*}:\mathbb{C}\to A,\quad 1\mapsto\sum_{g}|{\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{1}}\rangle,

(54)

and

\epsilon:A\to\mathbb{C},\quad|{\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{1}}\rangle\mapsto 1

(55)

By definition (
22
), a finite group
\mathrm{Aut}(A)
can be reconstructed:

\mathrm{Aut}(A)=\{\pi^{L}(\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{1}),g\in G\},

(56)

where
\pi^{L}
is defined to be

\pi^{L}(\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{h})\left|{\mathrm{A}^{g^{\prime}}\mathrm{B}^{h^{\prime}}}\right\rangle=\left|{\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{h}\mathrm{A}^{g^{\prime}}\mathrm{B}^{h^{\prime}}}\right\rangle.

(57)

Note that since any left multiplication commutes with a right multiplication,
\pi^{L}(\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{1})
is a morphism of
(A,\pi^{R})\to(A,\pi^{R})
. We shall not distinguish
G
from
\mathrm{Aut}(A)
, where
\pi^{L}(\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{1})
is identified with
g
since it defines a regular representation of
G
with
A
being the representation space.

The multiplication restricted to
\Delta^{*}:A\otimes V_{h}\to V_{h}
is commutative:

(58)

which defines
(V_{h},\Delta^{*})
as an
A
-module with
\Delta^{*}:A\otimes V_{h}\to V_{h}
being the module action. By dimension counting,
L_{\mathrm{Rep}A}=\{(V_{h},\Delta^{*})\}_{h\in G}
is a complete set of (representatives of) the simple objects in
\mathrm{Rep}A
.

The tensor product carries a group structure:

V_{g}\otimes_{A}V_{h}=V_{gh},

(59)

\mathrm{\mathbf{gr}}V_{g}=g.

(60)

Computing
\mathrm{\mathbf{gr}}(V_{g})
involves the braiding in
\mathrm{Rep}_{D^{\omega}(G)}
defined by
c_{V_{h_{1}},V_{h_{2}}}=\Sigma_{V_{h_{1}},V_{h_{2}}}\circ(\pi^{R}\otimes\pi^{R})(R)
, where
\Sigma_{(V_{h_{1}},,\pi^{R}),(V_{h_{2}},,\pi^{R})}
is the flip
v\otimes w\mapsto w\otimes v
, and
R
is the universal
R
matrix in Eq. (
201
).

(V_{h},\Delta^{*})\in L_{\mathrm{Rep}A}
, we define

(62)

where in the second equality we used the commutativity
\pi^{L}(\mathrm{A}^{g})\circ\Delta^{*}=\Delta^{*}\circ\pi^{L}(\Delta(\mathrm{A}^{g}))
.

Using Eq. (
196
), we have

u_{g_{1}}u_{g_{2}}=\beta_{h}(g_{1},g_{2})u_{g_{1}g_{2}}:V_{h}\to V_{g_{1}g_{2}hg_{1}^{-1}g_{2}^{-1}}.

(63)

The group action
T:\underline{G}\to\mathrm{Aut}_{\otimes}(\mathcal{C})
is given as follows. Define the functor
T_{g}:\mathrm{Rep}A\to\mathrm{Rep}A
by
T_{g}(V_{h},\Delta^{*})=(V_{h},\Delta^{*\overline{g}})
and
T_{g}(f)=f
. The tensor structure on
T_{g}
is defined by

\mu_{g}(x,y)\mathrm{id}_{V_{x}{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}V_{y}}:T_{g}(V_{x}{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}V_{y})\to T_{g}(V_{x}){\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}T_{g}(V_{y}).

(64)

The tensor structure on the the functor
T_{g}
is defined by

\beta_{x}(g,h)^{-1}\mathrm{id}_{V_{x}}:T_{gh}(V_{x})\to(T_{g}\circ T_{h})(V_{x}).

(65)

In summary, we have shown that
\mathrm{Rep}A\cong Vect^{\omega}_{G}
, where
Vect^{\omega}_{G}
is the category of finite dimensional
G
-graded vector spaces with an associativity
\omega\in H^{3}[G,U(1)]
. With the group action
T
, the equivariant structure
u_{g}=\pi^{L}(\mathrm{A}^{g})
.

5.1
Effective model

We have explicitly constructed the group action
T
and the equivariant structure
u_{g}
. Using these structures, we can write down the effective Hamiltonian. The Hilbert space is spanned by the basis

\left|{\mathrm{B}^{1}\mathrm{A}^{g_{0}};\mathrm{B}^{h_{1}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{1}},\mathrm{B}^{h_{2}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{2}},\dots,\mathrm{B}^{h_{N}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{N}}}\right\rangle.

(66)

The effective Hamiltonian is

H=-\sum_{n}Q_{n}-\lambda\sum_{n}W_{n},

(67)

where

Q_{n}\left|{\mathrm{B}^{1}\mathrm{A}^{g_{0}};\mathrm{B}^{h_{1}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{1}},\dots,\mathrm{B}^{h_{N}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{N}}}\right\rangle=\delta_{h_{n},1}\left|{\mathrm{B}^{1}\mathrm{A}^{g_{0}};\mathrm{B}^{h_{1}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{1}},\dots,\mathrm{B}^{h_{N}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{N}}}\right\rangle,

(68)

and

W_{n}\left|{\mathrm{B}^{1}\mathrm{A}^{g_{0}};\mathrm{B}^{h_{1}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{1}},\dots,\mathrm{B}^{h_{N}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{N}}}\right\rangle=\delta_{g_{n},g_{0}}\left|{\mathrm{B}^{1}\mathrm{A}^{g_{0}};\mathrm{B}^{h_{1}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{1}},\dots,\mathrm{B}^{h_{N}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{N}}}\right\rangle.

(69)

The ground states are
\left|{\mathrm{B}^{1}\mathrm{A}^{g};\mathrm{B}^{1}\mathrm{A}^{g},\dots,\mathrm{B}^{1}\mathrm{A}^{g}}\right\rangle
. The actual ground state with a fixed
g
will be chosen randomly by the system.

According to Definition (
37
) of the global symmetry transformation
U_{g}
, we have

U_{g}\left|{\mathrm{B}^{1}\mathrm{A}^{g_{0}};\mathrm{B}^{h_{1}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{1}},\dots,\mathrm{B}^{h_{N}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{N}}}\right\rangle=\pi^{R}\left(\Delta^{N}(\mathrm{A}^{g})\right)\left|{\mathrm{B}^{1}\mathrm{A}^{g_{0}};\mathrm{B}^{h_{1}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{1}},\dots,\mathrm{B}^{h_{N}}\mathrm{A}^{g_{N}}}\right\rangle,

(70)

where
\Delta^{N}=(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}^{\otimes{(N-1)}})\circ(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}^{\otimes{(N-2)}})\circ\dots\circ(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ\Delta
.

5.2
Example:
G=S_{3}

The simplest non-Abelian group is
G=S_{3}=(r,s|r^{3},s^{2})
. There are three irreducible representations denoted by
j_{0}
,
j_{1}
and
j_{2}
, with dimensions
\dim j_{0}=1
,
\dim j_{1}=1
, and
j_{2}=2
.

The twisted quantum double
D^{\omega}S_{3}
has eight irreducible representations. See Section
D.2
for the detailed construction of these representations. They are classified by the three conjugacy classes of
S_{3}
, denoted by
C_{1}=\{1\}
,
C_{2}=\{r,r^{2}\}
, and
C_{3}=\{s,rs,r^{2}s\}
. We denote by
j_{0},j_{1},j_{2}
the irreducible projective representations of
Z_{1}=S_{3}
, by
\theta_{0},\theta_{1},\theta_{2}
of
Z_{r}=\mathbb{Z}_{3}
, and by
\mu_{0},\mu_{1}
of
Z_{s}=\mathbb{Z}_{2}
, where
Z_{h}=\{g\in G|gh=hg\}
is the centralizer. The eight irreducible representations of
D^{\omega}G
are labeled by
(C_{1},j_{0})
,
(C_{1},j_{1})
,
(C_{1},j_{2})
,
(C_{2},\theta_{0})
,
(C_{2},\theta_{1})
,
(C_{2},\theta_{2})
,
(C_{3},\mu_{0})
, and
(C_{3},\mu_{1})
, respectively.

The Frobenius algebra
A
and
\mathrm{Rep}A
can be expressed in terms of these irreducible representations. Let
A=(C_{1},j_{0})\oplus(C_{1},j_{1})\oplus(C_{1},j_{2})\oplus(C_{1},j_{2})
. Label the vectors in
A
by
\left|{alpha;j,\beta}\right\rangle
, where
\alpha
is the multiplicity index of
j
appearing in
A
, and
\left|{j,\beta}\right\rangle
is the basis vectors of the representation space of
j
.

There are six simple objects in
\mathrm{Rep}A
:

\displaystyle V_{1}=A=(C_{1},j_{0})\oplus(C_{1},j_{1})\oplus(C_{1},j_{2})\oplus(C_{1},j_{2}),

(71)

\displaystyle V_{r}=(C_{2},\theta_{0})\oplus(C_{2},\theta_{1})\oplus(C_{2},\theta_{2}),

\displaystyle V_{r^{2}}=(C_{2},\theta_{0})\oplus(C_{2},\theta_{1})\oplus(C_{2},\theta_{2}),

\displaystyle V_{s}=(C_{3},\mu_{0})\oplus(C_{3},\mu_{1}),

\displaystyle V_{rs}=(C_{3},\mu_{0})\oplus(C_{3},\mu_{1}),

\displaystyle V_{r^{2}s}=(C_{3},\mu_{0})\oplus(C_{3},\mu_{1}).

The action
g:A\to A
is given by

g\left|{\alpha;j,\beta}\right\rangle=\sum_{\alpha^{\prime}}\rho^{j}_{\alpha^{\prime}\alpha}(g)\left|{\alpha^{\prime};j,\beta}\right\rangle,

(72)

where
\rho^{j}
is the representation matrix of
g
. The global symmetry transforms under the representation
\pi^{C}_{\mu}
defined in Eq. (
207
) of Appendix
D.2
.

6
Classification of maximal condensations in twisted quantum double phases

We have discussed charge condensation in twisted quantum double phases with a finite group
G
. In this section, we consider more generic condensation in a twisted quantum double phase where the condensation anyons are dyons (charge-flux composite). We consider the cases with a maximal (
{\dim_{\mathcal{C}}}A=|G|
) absorbing commutative Frobenius algebra. We call such condensation a maximal bosonic condensation. The resulting condensed phase is an SPT phase.

6.1
Quantum double phases

Let
\mathcal{C}=\mathrm{Rep}(D(G))
with
G
a finite group. The complete set of (representatives of) simple objects is denoted by

L_{\mathrm{Rep}(D(X))}=\{(a,\alpha)\}

(73)

where
a
is the representative of every conjugacy class of
G
, and
\alpha
is an irreducible representation of the centralizer
Z_{a}=\{z\in G|za=az\}
. The
S
-matrix and the twist
Coste et al. 2000
are

S_{(a,\alpha),(b,\beta)}=\frac{|G|}{|Z_{a}||Z_{b}|}\sum_{g\in G(a,b)}\bar{\chi}_{\alpha}(gb\overline{g})\bar{\chi}_{\beta}(\overline{g}ag)

(74)

\theta(a,\alpha)=\frac{\chi(a)}{\dim_{\alpha}}

(75)

where

G(a,b)=\{g\in G|agb\overline{g}=gb\overline{g}a\}.

(76)

The maximal bosonic condensations are classified by the absorbing commutative Frobenius algebras with with
{\dim_{\mathcal{C}}}A=|G|
. The full subcategory generated by such
A
is a Lagrangian subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
. (A Lagrangian subcategory is a symmetric subcategory
\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{C}
such that every
U\in\mathcal{C}
but
U\notin\mathcal{S}
has a nontrivial monodromy with
\mathcal{S}
).

The Lagrangian subcategories of
\mathcal{C}=\mathrm{Rep}(D(G))
are characterized by
(N,B)
, where
N\subset G
is an Abelian normal subgroup of
G
, and
B:N\times N\to U(1)
is a
G
-invariant alternating bicharacter on
N
, satisfying

\displaystyle B(h_{1}h_{2},h)=B(h_{1},h)B(h_{2},h),

(77)

\displaystyle B(h,h_{1}h_{2})=B(h,h_{1})B(h,h_{2}),

\displaystyle B(h,h)=1,

for all
h,h_{1},h_{2}\in N
, and the
G
-invariance condition

B(h_{1},h_{2})=B(gh_{1}\overline{g},gh_{2}\overline{g}).

(78)

Note that the above defining properties infer that
B(h_{1},h_{2})B(h_{2},h_{1})=1
.

Explicitly, the Lagrangian subcategory
\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}
is generated by

L_{\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}}=\left\{(a,\alpha)\in L_{\mathrm{Rep}(D(G))}\left|a\in N,\chi_{\alpha}(h)=B(a,h)\dim_{\alpha},\forall h\in N\right.\right\}

(79)

The Frobenius algebra
A
is then

A=\bigoplus_{j\in L_{\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}}}j^{\oplus{\dim_{\mathcal{C}}}(j)}.

(80)

The proof is given in Ref
Naidu and Nikshych 2008
, which is sketched in what follows.

The subcategory
\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}
is Lagrangian if
\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}
is symmetric with
\theta_{(a,\alpha)}=1
for every
(a,\alpha)\in L_{\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}}
, and
\dim\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}=|G|
. We first rewrite the condition that
\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}
is symmetric. By Ref
Müger 2003
, we need to verify that for all
(a,\alpha),(b,\beta)
, the
S
-matrix satisfies

S_{(a,\alpha),(b,\beta)}=\dim(a,\alpha)\dim(b,\beta)=|C_{a}|\dim_{\alpha}|C_{b}|\dim_{\beta}.

(81)

Plug Eq. (
77
) in, Eq. (
81
) is equivalent to the following two conditions:

1.

The conjugacy classes
C_{a}
and
C_{b}
commute element-wise.

2.

\chi_{\alpha}(gb\overline{g})\chi_{\beta}(\overline{g}ag)=\dim_{\alpha}\dim_{\beta}
, for all
g\in G
.

We check that
L_{\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}}
satisfies these two conditions. The first one is straightforward since
N
is an Abelian normal subgroup. The second can be verified directly using the defining properties of
B
:

\chi_{\alpha}(gb\overline{g})\chi_{\beta}(\overline{g}ag)=B(a,gb\overline{g})B(gb\overline{g},a)\dim_{\alpha}\dim_{\beta}=\dim_{\alpha}\dim_{\beta}.

(82)

Also, we compute
\theta_{(a,\alpha)}=\frac{\chi_{\alpha}(a)}{\dim_{\alpha}}\dim_{\alpha}=1
.

Finally,

\displaystyle\dim{\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}}=

\displaystyle\sum_{(a,\alpha)\in L_{\mathrm{Rep}(D(G))}}\dim(a,\alpha)^{2}

(83)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{a\in N\cap R}|C_{a}|^{2}\sum_{\alpha:\chi_{\alpha}(h)=B(a,h)\dim_{\alpha}\forall h\in N}\dim_{\alpha}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{a\in N\cap R}|C_{a}|^{2}\frac{|Z_{a}|}{|N|}=|G|,

where in the third equality, use is made of Clifford’s theorem and Frobenius reciprocity (see Ref
Naidu and Nikshych 2008
for a detailed proof), and the last equality holds since
N
is a normal subgroup.

6.2
Twisted quantum double phases

The complete set of (representatives of) simple objects in
\mathcal{C}=\mathrm{Rep}(D^{\omega}(G))
is denoted by

L_{\mathrm{Rep}(D^{\omega}(G))}=\{(a,\alpha)\},

(84)

where
a
is the representative of every conjugacy class of
G
, and
\alpha
is an irreducible
\beta_{a}
-representation of the centralizer
Z_{a}=\{z\in G|za=az\}
. By a
\beta_{a}
-representation we mean a projective representation such that
\rho(z)\rho(z^{\prime})=\beta_{a}(z,z^{\prime})\rho(zz^{\prime})
.

The
S
-matrix and the twist
Coste et al. 2000
are

\displaystyle S_{(a,\alpha),(b,\beta)}

(85)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{g\in C_{a},g^{\prime}\in C_{b}:gg^{\prime}=g^{\prime}g}\overline{\left(\frac{\beta_{a}(x,g^{\prime})\beta_{a}(xg^{\prime},x^{-1})\beta_{b}(y,g)\beta_{b}(yg,y^{-1})}{\beta_{b}(x,x^{-1})\beta_{b}(y,y^{-1})}\right)}\bar{\chi}_{\alpha}(xg^{\prime}x^{-1})\bar{\chi}_{\beta}(ygy^{-1})

and

\theta(a,\alpha)=\frac{\chi(a)}{\dim_{\alpha}},

(86)

where
x,y
are uniquely determined by
g=x^{-1}ax,g^{\prime}=y^{-1}by
.

Similar to the untwisted case, the Lagrangian subcategories of
\mathcal{C}=\mathrm{Rep}(D(G))
are characterized by
(N,B)
, where
N\subset G
is an Abelian normal subgroup of
G
, and
B:N\times N\to U(1)
is a
G
-invariant alternating
\omega
-bicharacter on
N
, satisfying

\displaystyle B(h_{1}h_{2},h)=\beta_{h}(h_{1},h_{2})B(h_{1},h)B(h_{2},h),

(87)

\displaystyle\beta_{h}(h_{1},h_{2})B(h,h_{1}h_{2})=B(h,h_{1})B(h,h_{2}),

\displaystyle B(h,h)=1,

for all
h,h_{1},h_{2}\in N
, and the
G
-invariance condition

B(x^{-1}ax,h)=\frac{\beta_{a}(x,h)\beta_{a}(xh,x^{-1})}{\beta_{a}(x,x^{-1})}B(a,xhx^{-1}),

(88)

for all
x\in G,a\in N\cup R,h\in N
.

The Lagrangian subcategory
\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}
is generated by

L_{\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}}=\left\{(a,\alpha)\in L_{\mathrm{Rep}(D^{\omega}(X))}\left|a\in N,\chi_{\alpha}(h)=B(a,h)\dim_{\alpha},\forall h\in N\right.\right\}.

(89)

The proof
Naidu and Nikshych 2008
is similar to that in the untwisted case. For
(a,\alpha),(b,\beta)\in L_{\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}}
, one can show that

S_{(a,\alpha),(b,\beta)}=\dim(a,\alpha)\dim(b,\beta)=|C_{a}|\dim_{\alpha}|C_{b}|\dim_{\beta},

(90)

which verifies
\theta_{(a,\alpha)}=\frac{\chi_{\alpha}(a)}{\dim_{\alpha}}\dim_{\alpha}=1
, and then computes

\dim{\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}}=|G|.

(91)

6.3
Global symmetry and Partial Electric-Magnetic duality

We will show that every maximal bosonic condensation in a twisted quantum double phase is equivalent to a pure charge condensation.

Let
\mathcal{C}=\mathrm{Rep}(D^{\omega}G)
be the modular tensor category characterizing a twisted quantum double phase. For every maximal bosonic condensation in
\mathcal{C}
, there is a Lagrange subcategory
\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}
with a normal Abelian subgroup
N
and an alternating function
B
.

The hidden global symmetry
X=\mathrm{Aut}(A)
is different from
G
if
N\neq\{1\}
. Then
\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}=\mathrm{Rep}_{X}
. The group structure of
X
is determined by the following properties:

1.

The
G
can be written as a semidirect product
G=N\rtimes_{F}K
, where
F\in H^{2}(K,N)
is a
2
-cocycle. The 3-cocycle can be expressed
Uribe Jongbloed 2017
explicitly (up to a coboundary) as

\omega((a_{1},k_{1}),(a_{2},k_{2}),(a_{3},k_{3}))=\hat{F}(k_{1},k_{2})(a_{3})\epsilon(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}),

(92)

where
\hat{F}\in H^{2}(K,\hat{N})
is a 2-cocycle, and
\epsilon\in C^{3}(K,U(1))
satisfies
\delta_{K}\epsilon=\hat{F}\land F
, i.e.,

\delta_{K}\epsilon(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4})=\frac{\epsilon(k_{2},k_{3},k_{4})\epsilon(k_{1},k_{2}k_{3},k_{4})\epsilon(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})}{\epsilon(k_{1}k_{2},k_{3},k_{4})\epsilon(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}k_{4})}=\hat{F}(k_{1},k_{2})(F(k_{3},k_{4})).

(93)

2.

The
X
can be written as
X=K\ltimes_{\hat{F}}\hat{N}
. Here
\hat{N}
is the Abelian group whose elements are the unitary irreducible representations of
N
.

Define
\omega^{\prime}\in H^{3}(G^{\prime},U(1))
by

\omega^{\prime}((x_{1},\rho_{1}),(x_{2},\rho_{2}),(x_{3},\rho_{3}))=\rho_{1}(F(x_{2},x_{3}))\epsilon(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}).

(94)

Then
\mathrm{Rep}(D^{\omega}G)\cong\mathrm{Rep}(D^{\omega^{\prime}}X)
(
Naidu 2010
;
Uribe Jongbloed 2017
).

According to Ref
Hu and Wan 2020
, such an equivalence is realized by a partial electric-magnetic duality, under the Fourier transform
N\to\hat{N}
. The condensate anyons form the complete set
L_{\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}}
of composites of pure
N
-flux and
K
-charge. Under the partial electric-magnetic duality, they become pure
(K\ltimes_{\hat{F}}\hat{N})
-charges. Indeed, the condensate anyons form the set

L_{\mathcal{L}_{(N,B)}}=\left\{(a,\alpha)\in L_{\mathrm{Rep}(D^{\omega}(X))}\left|a\in N,\chi_{\alpha}(h)=\dim_{\alpha},\forall h\in N\right.\right\}.

(95)

The condensate anyons range over all possible all
N
-fluxes
a\in N
, and contains no
N
-charge according to the condition
\chi_{\alpha}(h)=\dim_{\alpha}
. Hence they are the set of composites of pure
N
-flux and
K
-charge.

The global symmetry transformation can be derived from the EM duality. The isomorphism
Hu and Wan 2020

D^{\alpha}G\rightarrow D^{\alpha^{\prime}}X
is given by

A^{(a,x)}B^{(b,y)}\mapsto\frac{1}{|N|}\sum_{\rho,\eta\in\hat{N}}\rho(a)\overline{\eta(b)}\ \tilde{B}^{\left(xy\bar{x},\rho\right)}\tilde{A}^{(x,\eta)},

(96)

where
(a,x),(b,y)
are group elements of
G
and
\left(xy\bar{x},\rho\right),(x,\eta)
of
X
.

Hence the group elements of
X
is expressed in terms of elements of
D^{\omega^{\prime}}X
:

\tilde{\mathrm{A}}^{(x,\eta)}=\frac{1}{|N|}\sum_{b\in N,y\in K}\eta(b)\mathrm{A}^{(1,x)}\mathrm{B}^{(b,y)}.

(97)

The global symmetry transformation and the effective theory are constructed in a similar way as in Section
5
.

6.4
Example for
G=D_{m}

The simplest non-Abelian group is the symmetric group
S_{3}
, or the Dihedral group
D_{3}
. Denote the elements of
D_{3}
by
(A,a)
, for
A=0,1
and
a=0,1,\dotsc,m
, where
m=3
for
D_{3}
case. The multiplication is given by

(A,a)\circ(B,b)=\left(\langle A+B\rangle_{2},\langle(-1)^{B}a+b\rangle_{m}\right)

(98)

where
\langle n\rangle_{m}
stands for
n\ \mathrm{mod}\ m
.

For convenience, we rewrite
(A,a)
as
A_{a}
for short. Define the 3-cocycle
\omega
by

\omega(A_{a},B_{b},C_{c})=\exp\left\{\frac{2\pi i}{m^{2}}\left[(-1)^{B+C}a\left((-1)^{C}b+c-\langle(-1)^{C}b+c\rangle_{m}\right)+\frac{m^{2}}{2}ABC\right]\right\}.

(99)

It generates 3-cocycle representatives
\omega^{k}
for all other cohomology classes
k=0,1,\dotsc,2m-1
.

For
m=3
, there are 8 irreducible representations of
D^{\omega}(G)
, namely

K_{1}=\{0_{0}\}

\rho_{0}

\rho_{1}

\rho_{2}

K_{2}=\{0_{1},0_{2}\}

\mu_{0}

\mu_{1}

\mu_{2}

K_{3}=\{1_{0},1_{1},1_{2}\}

\nu_{0}

\nu_{1}

where
\rho_{0},\rho_{1},\rho_{2}
are the three irreducible representations of the centralizer
Z_{e}=S_{3}
,
\mu_{0},\mu_{1},\mu_{2}
are the three irreducible projective representations of
Z_{0_{1}}=\mathbb{Z}_{3}
(with
\mu_{0}
being the trivial one), and
\nu_{0},\nu_{1}
are the two irreducible projective representations of
Z_{1_{0}}=\mathbb{Z}_{2}
(with
\nu_{0}
being the trivial one).

The Abelian normal subgroups
N
of
S_{3}
is either
K_{1}=\{0_{0}\}
or
K_{1}\sqcup K_{2}=\{0_{0},0_{1},0_{2}\}
. For
N=K_{1}=\{0_{0}\}
, the Lagrangian subcategory is generated by
\rho_{0},\rho_{1},\rho_{2}
, i.e., all irreducible representations of
S_{3}
. The corresponding Frobenius algebra is
A=\rho_{0}\oplus\rho_{1}\oplus\rho_{2}\oplus\rho_{2}
.

For
N=K_{1}\sqcup K_{2}=\{0_{0},0_{1},0_{2}\}
, the solution to the alternating bicharacter exits iff
\omega=1
. The only solution is
B(h_{1},h_{2})=1
for all
h_{1},h_{2}\in N
. Hence are those From
\rho_{0},\rho_{1},\rho_{2},\mu_{0},\mu_{1},\mu_{2}
, we pick up
\rho_{0},\rho_{1},\mu_{0}
as the generating objects of the Lagranginan subcategory, which satisfying
\rho(h)=\mathrm{id}
for
h\in N
. Hence the Frobenius algebra is
A=\rho_{0}\oplus\rho_{1}\oplus\mu_{0}\oplus\mu_{0}
. The group
X=\mathrm{Aut}(A)
turns out to be
X=D_{3}
(In fact,
D_{3}
is the only group that can have irreducible representations
\rho_{0},\rho_{1},\mu_{0}
). Note that
X=D_{3}
is different from
G=D_{3}
. The anyon condensation in the phase
\mathrm{Rep}(D(G))
for
G=D_{3}
will results in a SPT phase with global symmetry
X=D_{3}
.

The equivalence
\mathrm{Rep}(D(D_{4}))\cong\mathrm{Rep}\left(D^{\omega^{\prime}}(\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2})\right)
is known widely for certain
\omega^{\prime}\in H^{3}[\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2},U(1)]
. All other normal Abelian subgroups of
\mathrm{Rep}(D(D_{4}))
give rise to a global symmetry group
X=D_{4}
.

In general, for
G=D_{m}
with
m\geqslant 5
, the normal Abelian subgroups of
G
are precisely the rotation subgroups
\mathbb{Z}_{m/k}
generated by
0_{k}
, where
k
is a divisor of
m
. The Lagrangian subcategories are equivalent to
\mathrm{Rep}(Dih(N))
, where
N=\mathbb{Z}_{m/k}\times\mathbb{Z}_{k}
, and
Dih(N)=N\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}
is the generalized Dihedral group for an Abelian group
N
, with
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
acting on
N
by inverting elements. The anyon condensation will result in a SPT phase, with a global symmetry
X=\mathbb{Z}_{m/k}\times\mathbb{Z}_{k}
.

7
Restore hidden symmetry: gauging symmetry enriched topological phases

We have discussed the effective theory of complete anyon condensation. The condensed phase is described by coherent states using
(\mathrm{Rep}A)^{G}
(in terms of the simple objects in
\mathrm{Rep}A
).

We consider a reversed process of condensation: How can we restore the hidden symmetry? We can introduce a gauge invariance term in the Hamiltonian:

-J\sum_{n}T_{n},

(100)

where
J>0
and
T_{n}
acts on the basis vectors (
30
) by

T_{n}\left|{g_{N}V_{N}}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g}\left(u_{g}+u_{g}^{\dagger}\right)\left|{g_{N}V_{N}}\right\rangle.

(101)

The
T_{n}
does not commute with
W_{n}
. When
J\gg\lambda
, the energy eiegenstates have basis vectors in Eq. (
21
).

The topological charge of anyons are no longer simple objects in
\mathrm{Rep}A
but those in
(\mathrm{Rep}A)^{G}
. It is known
Kirillov and Ostrik 2002
;
Müger 2004
, that
(\mathrm{Rep}A)^{G}\cong\mathcal{C}
; hence, we restore the parent phase characterized by
\mathcal{C}
.

Appendix A
Frobenius algebra and its modules

This appendix consists some preliminary mathematics of a Frobenius algebra and its modules. To be clear, instead of containing complete proofs for every statement, we just intend to provide enough computational tools to support the paper.

We start with strict tensor categories. The standard definitions of tensor categories can be found in cf. the standard reference
Mac Lane 1998
. A tensor category is strict if its tensor product satisfies associativity
(X\otimes Y)\otimes Z=X\otimes(Y\otimes Z)
on the nose and its unit object
\boldsymbol{1}
satisfies
X\otimes\boldsymbol{1}=\boldsymbol{1}\otimes X=X
for all
X
. Throughout the paper, we assume the categories over
\mathds{C}
are always Abelian.

In our convention, we represent morphisms in a tensor category by tangle diagrams. These diagrams are drawn to be read from the bottom to the top. With

a:X\rightarrow Y,b:Y\rightarrow Z,c:U\rightarrow V,d:V\rightarrow W
, we represent

b\otimes d\circ a\otimes c=(b\circ a)\otimes(d\circ c)\in\mathrm{Hom}(X\otimes U,Z\otimes W)

by

The
Y
is a subobject of
X
, if there are morphisms
e:X\rightarrow Y,f:Y\rightarrow X
such that
e\circ f=\mathrm{id}_{X}
, and
p=f\circ e\in\mathrm{End}(X)
is an idempotent, i.e.,
p^{2}=p
. We denote
Y
arising from the
X
and
p
by
{X\!\left|{}_{p}\right.}
. If every idempotent in a category
\mathcal{C}
arises in this way, we say ‘idempotents split in
\mathcal{C}
’ or ‘
\mathcal{C}
has subobjects’.

A.1
Frobenius algebra

Assume
\mathcal{C}
is a modular tensor category. So
\mathcal{C}
has two-sided duals. This means, for every
X\in\mathcal{C}
, there exists a
X^{*}\in\mathcal{C}
together with rigidity morphisms
e_{X}:\boldsymbol{1}\rightarrow X\otimes X^{*},d_{X}:X^{*}\otimes X\rightarrow\boldsymbol{1},\varepsilon_{X}:\boldsymbol{1}\rightarrow X^{*}\otimes X,\eta_{X}:X\otimes X^{*}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{1}
, depicted by the diagrams:

(106)

The second equality holds because
\mathcal{C}
is pivotal and semisimple.

In categrory
\mathcal{C}
, one can define Forbenius algebras. In
\mathcal{C}
, a Frobenius algebra
A
is a quintuple
(A,\mu,\Delta,\iota,\epsilon)
, where
A
is an object and

\iota:\boldsymbol{1}\rightarrow A,\epsilon:A\rightarrow\boldsymbol{1},\Delta:A\rightarrow A\otimes A,\mu:A\otimes A\rightarrow A

are morphisms. These morphisms should satisfy the following conditions:

\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}_{A}\,\circ\,\Delta=\mathrm{id}_{A}\otimes\Delta\,\circ\,\Delta,

(107)

\mu\,\circ\,\mu\otimes\mathrm{id}_{A}=\mu\,\circ\,\mathrm{id}_{A}\otimes\mu,

(108)

\epsilon\otimes\mathrm{id}_{A}\,\circ\,\Delta=\mathrm{id}_{A}=\mathrm{id}_{A}\otimes\epsilon\,\circ\,\Delta,

(109)

\mu\,\circ\,\iota\otimes\mathrm{id}_{A}=\mathrm{id}_{A}=\mu\,\circ\,\mathrm{id}_{A}\otimes\iota,

(110)

\mu\otimes\mathrm{id}_{A}\,\circ\,\mathrm{id}_{A}\otimes\Delta=\Delta\,\circ\,\mu=\mathrm{id}_{A}\otimes\mu\,\circ\,\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}_{A}.

(111)

, their tensor product

(129)

since the left hand side is a morphism in
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Rep}A}(A,A)=\mathds{C}
,
\dim_{A}V\in\mathds{C}
. Using Eq. (
116
), we see that

{\dim_{A}}V=\frac{{\dim_{\mathcal{C}}}V}{{\dim_{\mathcal{C}}}A}.

(130)

The quantum dimension of the tensor product
(V{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}W,\rho_{V}{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}\rho_{W})
can be computed by

{\dim_{A}}(V{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}W)=\frac{\dim_{\mathcal{C}}(V{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}W)}{{\dim_{\mathcal{C}}}A}=\frac{{\dim_{\mathcal{C}}}V{\dim_{\mathcal{C}}}W}{({\dim_{\mathcal{C}}}A)^{2}}={\dim_{A}}V{\dim_{A}}W,

(131)

where in the second equality we computed

F

by

f=
\frac{1}{{\dim_{\mathcal{C}}}A}
V
V

(135)

satisfying that
e\circ f=\mathrm{id}_{V}
and that
f\circ e
being an idempotent. Hence, all objects in
\mathrm{Rep}A
are subobjects of
FX
for some

(137)

Every idempotent
FX\to FX
must be in the form
\overline{p}
for some
p:A\otimes X\rightarrow X
, according to the property (
122
). Every
(V,\rho)\in\mathrm{Rep}A
can be identified with
{FV\!\left|{}_{\frac{1}{{\dim_{\mathcal{C}}}A}\,\overline{\rho}}\right.}
in the canonical way (
135
).

Simple objects are now written as
{FX\!\left|{}_{\overline{p}}\right.}
where
\overline{p}:FX\rightarrow FX
is a minimal idempotent (namely,
\overline{p}
can not be
\overline{p_{1}}+\overline{p_{2}}
for
\overline{p_{1}}\neq 0
and
\overline{p_{2}}\neq 0
). Particularly, the unit
(A,\mu)
is identified with
F\boldsymbol{1}|_{\overline{\epsilon}}
.

A useful property is

\mathrm{Hom}_{A}(FX,W)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,W),

(138)

for every
W\in\mathrm{Rep}A
and
X\in\mathcal{C}
. Indeed, every morphism
f\in\mathrm{Hom}_{A}(FX,W)
can be written uniquely in terms of a morphism in
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,W)
by

X
W
f
=
f
\frac{1}{{\dim_{\mathcal{C}}}A}
W
X
W

(139)

Particularly, for
X,Y\in\mathcal{C}
, we have

\mathrm{Hom}_{A}(FX,FY)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,A\otimes Y).

(140)

The image of
F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathrm{Rep}A
is equivalent to the pre-quotient category
\mathcal{C}/A
, whose objects are those of
\mathcal{C}
, and whose morphisms are

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}/A}(X,Y)=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,A\otimes Y).

(141)

When the objects are equipped with idempotents, they form the quotient category.

Appendix B
Reconstruction theorem: finite group
G=\mathrm{Aut}A
from the absorbing Frobenius algebra

When
A
is absorbing (to be defined below), we can reconstruct
Deligne 2007
;
Müger 2004
a finite group
G
such that
A
is equivalent to the regular representation of
G
.

The
A
is
absorbing
if

(A,\mu)\otimes(A,\mu)=(A,\mu)^{\oplus N}

(142)

for some positive integer
N
. Let
\mathcal{S}
be the minimum full subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
containing
A
. In the means time, denote
L_{\mathcal{S}}\subset L_{\mathcal{C}}
as the subset of (isomorphism class of) simple objects in
\mathcal{S}
.

According Perron-Frobenius theorem,
A
must have the form

A=\bigoplus_{X_{j}\in L_{\mathcal{S}}}{X_{j}}^{\oplus\mathrm{PFdim}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_{j})},

(143)

where
\mathrm{PFdim}_{\mathcal{C}}X_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}
is the Penrron-Frobenius dimension. See Appendix
B.1
for the proof.

The
\mathcal{S}
is a symmetric tensor category since,
\forall X_{j}\in\mathcal{S}
,
\theta_{X_{j}}=\mathrm{id}_{X_{j}}
holds. In [Muger], they have constructed a fibre functor using
A
, which is used to reconstruct a finite group
G
such that
\mathcal{S}
is equivalent to the Tannakian representation category
\mathrm{Rep}_{G}
. We briefly review this reconstruction below.

The fibre functor
E:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathrm{Vect}
is constructed as follows. For every
X\in\mathcal{S}
, we define
EX=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(A,X)
, and
E(f)
for
f:X\rightarrow Y
by
E(f)\phi=f\circ\phi
for
\phi\in EX
. The tensor structure
\varphi_{X,Y}:EX\otimes EY\rightarrow E(X\otimes Y)
is given by

(153)

Because
|G|=\sum_{X_{j}\in L_{\mathcal{S}}}(\dim EX_{j})^{2}=\sum_{X_{j}\in L_{\mathcal{S}}}(\mathrm{PFdim}_{\mathcal{C}}X_{j})^{2}=\mathrm{PFdim}_{\mathcal{C}}A=\dim\mathrm{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(A)
, any of
\{g\in G\}
,
\{\alpha_{n}\}
and
\{\alpha^{*}_{n}\}
is a basis of
\mathrm{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(A)
. Hence
\alpha_{n}
and
\alpha_{n}^{*}
have linear expansions
\alpha_{n}=\sum_{g\in G}\alpha_{n}(g)g
and
\alpha^{*}_{n}=\sum_{h\in G}\alpha^{*}_{n}(h)h
for
\alpha_{n}(g),\alpha^{*}_{n}(h)\in\mathbb{C}
. Eqs. (
153
) imply

\mathrm{id}_{A}=\sum_{n}\alpha_{n}\circ\alpha^{*}_{n}=\sum_{g,h\in G}\left(\sum_{n}\alpha_{n}(g)\alpha^{*}_{n}(h)\right)gh,

(154)

which holds iff
\sum_{n}\alpha_{n}(g)\alpha^{*}_{n}(h)=\delta_{gh,1}/|G|
, and Eq. (
154
) leads to Eq. (
151
).

∎

A useful consequence is that any
\mathcal{C}
-morphism
f:A\rightarrow A\otimes A
can be decomposed as

f
g
g
f
=
\frac{1}{|G|}
\Sigma_{g}
=
g
x
\sum_{gx}f_{gx}

(155)

In the above reconstruction,
A
is interpreted as a left regular representation space of
G
, and the properties (
151
) and (
149
) are the usual orthonormal conditions in the representation theory.

B.1
Dimension Proof

Suppose the decomposition of
A
is

A=\bigoplus_{X_{j}\in L_{\mathcal{S}}}n_{j}X_{j},

(156)

where multiplicity
n_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}
, and
n_{\boldsymbol{1}}=1
.

The decomposition
A\otimes A=A^{\oplus N}
implies

\sum_{ij\in L_{\mathcal{S}}}N_{ij}^{k}n_{i}n_{j}=Nn_{k},

(157)

where
N_{ij}^{k}=\dim\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_{i}\otimes X_{j},X_{k})
. Define a
|L_{\mathcal{S}}|\times|L_{\mathcal{S}}|
matrix
R
whose matrix element is
R_{kj}=\sum_{i}N_{ij}^{k}n_{i}
. This
R
is strictly positive matrix (otherwise
N^{k}_{ij}=0
for all
i
). By Perron-Frobenius theorem, there is a unique eigenvector with strictly positive entries
n_{k}
. Using the normalization
n_{\boldsymbol{1}}=1
, the only solution is
n_{j}=\mathrm{PFdim}_{\mathcal{C}}X_{j}
, where
\mathrm{FPdim}Z_{j}
is the Frobenius-Perron dimension. This dimension is defined by the maximal non-negative eigenvalue of the matrix
N_{i}
whose matrix elements are
[N_{i}]_{jk}=N_{ij}^{k}
.

By everything mentioned above, we conclude that

A=\bigoplus_{X_{j}\in L_{\mathcal{S}}}{X_{j}}^{\oplus\mathrm{PFdim}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_{j})}.

(158)

Appendix C
Group Action and Equivariantization

C.1
Grading of
\mathrm{Rep}A
by
G=\mathrm{Aut}A

When
A
is absorbing, a finite group
G=\mathrm{Aut}(A)
is reconstructed. We review the
G
-grading of
\mathrm{Rep}A
.

Let
G
be a finite group. A
G
-graded fusion category
\mathcal{D}
is a fusion category endowed with pairwise disjoint subcategories
\{\mathcal{D}_{g}\}_{g\in G}
such that

(a)

every
X\in\mathcal{D}
splits as
X=\oplus_{g}X_{g}
where
X_{g}\in\mathcal{D}_{g}
;

(b)

if
X\in\mathcal{D}_{g},Y\in\mathcal{D}_{h}
, then
X\otimes Y\in\mathcal{D}_{gh}
;

(c)

if
X\in\mathcal{D}_{g},Y\in\mathcal{C}_{h}
with
g\neq h
, then
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(X,Y)=0
;

(d)

\boldsymbol{1}_{\mathcal{D}}\in\mathcal{D}_{1}
.

For
X\in\mathcal{D}_{g}
, we say
X
has the grading
\mathrm{\mathbf{gr}}X=g
. Note that condition (b) implies
\mathrm{\mathbf{gr}}(X^{*})=\mathrm{\mathbf{gr}}(X)^{-1}
, because
X\otimes X^{*}=\boldsymbol{1}_{\mathcal{D}}\oplus\dots
and
\mathrm{\mathbf{gr}}({\boldsymbol{1}_{\mathcal{D}}})=1
.

Let
\mathcal{D}=\mathrm{Rep}A
and
G=\mathrm{Aut}(A)
. Before constructing the
G
-grading, we introduce a useful idempotent
\pi_{g}:FX\to FX
,
X\in\mathcal{C}
:

(159)

It is possible that: (1)
\pi_{g}=0
, or (2)
\pi_{g}
is not minimal.

Proposition 2
.

If
p:FX\to FX
is a minimal idempotent, then there exists a unique
g\in G
such that
p\pi_{g}=p=\pi_{g}p
.

Proof.

Obviously,
\pi_{g}
is central:
\pi_{g}p=p\pi_{g}
. Also use
\sum_{g}\pi_{g}=\mathrm{id}_{A\otimes X}
and
\pi_{g}\pi_{h}=0
if
g\neq h
.
∎

For every simple
X\in\mathrm{Rep}A
, we define the grading by

C.2
Group action and Equivariantization

Using the
G=\mathrm{Aut}(A)
reconstructed from
A
, we will construct a group action and the equivariantization category
(\mathrm{Rep}A)^{G}
.

We briefly recall some notation on tensor categories. A tensor functor between two tensor categories
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
is
(F,\varphi,\varphi_{0})
where
F:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
is a functor,
\varphi:F\circ\otimes_{\mathcal{C}}\xrightarrow{\sim}\otimes_{\mathcal{D}}\circ(F\times F)
a natural isomorphism, and
\varphi_{0}:F(\boldsymbol{1}_{\mathcal{C}})\xrightarrow{\sim}\boldsymbol{1}_{\mathcal{D}}
is an isomorphism. We call
\varphi
the tensor structure on
F
and
\varphi_{0}
the unit-preserving structure on
F
. For a finite group
G
, let
\underline{G}
be the tensor category whose objects are elements of
G
, morphisms are the identities, and whose tensor product is given by the multiplication in
G
.

A group action on
\mathcal{C}
is
(T,\gamma,\iota,\mu,\nu)
where
T
is a tensor functor
T:\underline{G}\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut}_{\otimes}\mathcal{D};g\mapsto T_{g}
. The category
\underline{G}
has objects
g\in G
, and morphisms
\mathrm{Hom}(g,h)=\emptyset
if
g\neq h
and
\mathrm{Hom}(g,g)=\mathbb{C}
, with
\otimes
defined by
g\otimes h=gh
.
\mathrm{Aut}_{\otimes}\mathcal{D}
is the category of auto tensor functors
\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{D}
. The tensor structure and the unit-preserving structure on
T
are denoted by

\gamma_{g,h}:T_{gh}\xrightarrow{\sim}T_{g}\circ T_{h}

(172)

\iota:T_{e}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{C}}

(173)

for any
g,h\in G
. And
\{\mu_{g}\}
is a family of tensor structures on
T_{g}
,
\{\nu_{g}\}
a family of unit-preserving structures on
T_{g}
.

A
G
-
equivariant
object in
\mathcal{D}
is a pair
(X,\{u_{g}\}_{g\in G})
where
X\in\mathcal{D}
and
u_{g}:T_{g}X\to X
is a family of isomorphisms called
equivariant structure
on
X
such that

T_{gh}X
T_{g}T_{h}X
X
T_{g}X
\gamma_{gh}(X)
u_{gh}
T_{g}(u_{h})
u_{g}

(174)

for all
g,h\in G
.

The fusion category formed by the
G
-equivariant objects is called the
equivariantization
of
\mathcal{D}
, denoted by
\mathcal{D}^{G}
. The morphisms are those of
\mathcal{D}
that commute with
u_{g}
.

Let
L_{\mathrm{Rep}A}=\{(V,\rho_{V})\}
be the set of representatives of simple objects in
\mathrm{Rep}A
.

For every
(V,\rho_{V})\in\mathrm{Rep}A
, we define
T_{g}(V,\rho_{V})=(V,\rho_{V}^{\overline{g}})\in\mathrm{Rep}A
, where

(175)

If
(V,\rho_{V})
is simple,
T_{g}(V,\rho_{V})
is simple too.

Proposition 3
.

For every
(V,\rho_{V})\in L_{\mathrm{Rep}A}
and
g\in G
, there exits an object
(V,\rho^{\prime}_{V})\in L_{\mathrm{Rep}A}
, and a unique
\mathcal{C}
-isomorphism
u_{g}:V\to V
, such that

(179)

\alpha
to label the basis because
\mathrm{Hom}_{A}(U^{\prime},V^{\prime}{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}W^{\prime})\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{A}(U,V{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}W)
according Eq. (
178
). We require
\mu_{g}(U;V,W)(\alpha^{\prime})=\eta\alpha
for some nonzero complex number
\eta
.

(181)

Given Eq. (
181
), we can extend the definition
u_{g}
to generic objects of
\mathrm{Rep}A
. Using
u_{g}
, we define the group action and the equivariantization below.

For every
g\in G
, we define the tensor functor
T_{g}:\mathrm{Rep}A\to\mathrm{Rep}A
as follows.
Let
T^{g}(V,\rho_{V})=(V,\rho_{V}^{\overline{g}})
as defined in Eq. (
175
), and
T_{g}(f)=f
for
f\in\mathrm{Hom}_{A}(V,V)
. Define the tensor structure on
T_{g}
by
\mu_{g}(V,W):T_{g}(V{\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}W)\to T_{g}(V){\,\otimes\!_{A}\,}T_{g}(W)
as given in Eq. (
180
).

Then we define the group action
T:\underline{G}\to\mathrm{Aut}_{\otimes}(\mathrm{Rep}A)
, by defining the tensor structure on
T
by

\beta_{V}(g,h)^{-1}\mathrm{id}_{V}:T_{gh}V\to T_{g}T_{h}V,

(182)

where
\beta_{V}(g,h)
is defined in Eq. (
177
).

Now we claim
u_{g}:T_{g}V\to V
is an equivariant structure. The equivariantization cateogry
(\mathrm{Rep}A)^{G}
has objects
(V\in\mathrm{Rep}A,u_{g}:V\to V)
.

The grading under the group action is given by

\mathrm{\mathbf{gr}}(T_{g}X)=g\circ\mathrm{\mathbf{gr}}(X)\circ\overline{g}

(183)

which is verified by

(184)

C.2.1
Alternative Group action

Using the group action
T
has the advantage of nice properties in Eqs. (
145
)(
148
)(
149
). But
T_{g}(V,\rho_{V})\neq L_{\mathrm{Rep}A}
for any
(V,\rho_{V})
, hence
T
is not convenient for a computations in a tensor description. The equivariant structure
u_{g}
maps back
T_{g}(V,\rho_{V})
to some
(V,\rho^{\prime}_{V})\neq L_{\mathrm{Rep}A}
. Alternatively, one can define
T^{\prime}
by
T^{\prime}_{g}(V)=V^{\prime}
for every
V\in\mathrm{Rep}A
with
u_{g}:V\to V^{\prime}
, and
T_{g}(f)=u_{g}\circ f\circ u_{g}^{-1}
for every
A
-morphism
f
. We will not use this construction in this paper.

C.3
Concrete construction of the equivariant structure

In the following, we construct an explicit form of the equivariant structure
u_{g}
. For every
g
, we pick up a representative simple object in
L_{\mathrm{Rep}A}
with the grading
g
, denoted by
V_{g}
.

For every
W\in\mathrm{Rep}A
and every
g
, we have a projector

C.4
Orbits in
\mathrm{Rep}A
under the group action

Proposition 4
.

Simple objects of
\mathrm{Rep}A
has properties:

(i)

For simple
(V,\rho_{V})\in\mathrm{Rep}A
,
FV=\displaystyle\bigoplus_{g}T_{g}(V,\rho_{V})
.

(ii)

For simple
(V,\rho_{V}),(V,\rho^{\prime}_{V})\in\mathrm{Rep}A
, there exists a non-empty subgroup
K_{(V,\rho_{V})}\subseteq G
, such that
T_{g}(V,\rho_{V})=(V,\rho^{\prime}_{V})
for
g\in K_{(V,\rho_{V})}
, and
|K_{(V,\rho_{V})}|=\dim\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(V,V)
.

(iii)

For simple
(V,\rho_{V}),(W,\rho_{W})\in\mathrm{Rep}A
, either
V=W
or
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(V,W)=0
.

(ii)

Using Eq. (
138
), we have

\mathrm{Hom}_{A}\left(\bigoplus_{g}T_{g}(V,\rho_{V}),(V,\rho^{\prime}_{V})\right)=\mathrm{Hom}_{A}\left(FV,(V,\rho^{\prime}_{V})\right)=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(V,V)

(194)

(iii)

Suppose
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(V,W)\neq 0
. Then

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hom}_{A}(FV,(W,\rho_{W}))=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(V,W)\neq 0

\displaystyle\Rightarrow\quad

\displaystyle T_{g}(V,\rho_{V})=(W,\rho_{W})\text{ for some }g\in G

\displaystyle\Rightarrow\quad

\displaystyle V=W.

(195)

Appendix D
Twisted quantum double
D^{\omega}G
and its representations

D.1
Twisted quantum double
D^{\omega}G

In this section, we briefly review the definition of the twisted Drinfeld’s twisted double of a finite group
Dijkgraaf et al. 1991
as a quasi-triangular quasi-Hopf algebra. Let
D^{\alpha}G
be a finite-dimensional vector space with a basis
\{\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{x}\}_{(g,x)\in G\times G}
. Define a product on
D^{\alpha}G
by

(\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{x})(\mathrm{A}^{h}\mathrm{B}^{y}):=\delta_{x,hy\bar{h}}\beta_{y}(g,h)\mathrm{A}^{gh}\mathrm{B}^{y}.

(196)

We also use symbols
\mathrm{B}^{h}=\mathrm{A}^{1}\mathrm{B}^{h}
,
\mathrm{A}^{g}=\sum_{x}\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{x}
, and
\mathrm{B}^{h}\mathrm{A}^{g}=\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{\overline{g}hg}
for convenience.
The unit is

1=\sum_{x\in G}\mathrm{A}^{1}\mathrm{B}^{x}.

(197)

Define the coproduct
\Delta:D^{\alpha}G\rightarrow D^{\alpha}G\otimes D^{\alpha}G
and the counit
\varepsilon:D^{\alpha}G\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
by

\Delta(\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{x}):=\sum_{a,b\in G:ab=x}\mu_{g}(a,b)(\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{a})\otimes(\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{b})

(198)

and

\varepsilon(\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{x}):=\delta_{x,1}.

(199)

Besides, set the Drinfeld associator by

\Phi:=\sum_{x,y,z\in G}\alpha(x,y,z)^{-1}(\mathrm{A}^{1}\mathrm{B}^{x})\otimes(\mathrm{A}^{1}\mathrm{B}^{y})\otimes(\mathrm{A}^{1}\mathrm{B}^{z}),

(200)

and the
R
matrix
4
4

4

we choose
R
matrix to be compatible with formula in Section
5
by

R:=\sum_{x,y\in G}\frac{1}{\beta_{y}(x,x^{-1})}((\mathrm{A}^{x^{-1}})\mathrm{B}^{y})\otimes(\mathrm{A}^{1}\mathrm{B}^{x}).

(201)

Finally, define the antipode by a linear map
S:D^{\alpha}G\rightarrow D^{\alpha}G

S(\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{x}):=\frac{1}{\beta_{\bar{x}}\left({g},\bar{g}\right)\mu_{g}\left(x,\bar{x}\right)}\mathrm{A}^{\bar{g}}\mathrm{B}^{{g}\bar{x}\bar{g}},

(202)

where
\beta_{x}(g,h)
and
\mu_{g}(x,y)
are expressed in terms of
\alpha
by

\beta_{x}(g,h):=\frac{\alpha(g,h,x)\alpha\left(ghx\bar{h}\bar{g},g,h\right)}{\alpha\left(g,hx\bar{h},h\right)}

(203)

and

\mu_{g}(x,y):=\frac{\alpha\left(gx\bar{g},gy\bar{g},g\right)\alpha(g,x,y)}{\alpha\left(gx\bar{g},g,y\right)}

(204)

for all
g,h,x,y\in G
.

D.2
Representations

In this subsection, we review the simple objects in
\mathrm{Rep}(D^{\omega}G)
. For every conjugacy class
C
of
G
, we choose a representative member
h_{1}\in C
. We denote by
Z_{C}
the centralizer
\{z\in G|zh_{1}=h_{1}z\}
. We denote by
(\mu,V_{\mu})
the irreducible projective representations of
Z_{C}
with
\beta_{h_{1}}\in H^{2}(Z_{C},U(1))
:

\mu(z_{1})\mu(z_{2})=\beta_{h_{1}}(z_{1},z_{2})\mu(z_{1}z_{2}),

(205)

where
\beta
is defined by

\beta_{h_{1}}(z_{1},z_{2}):=\frac{\omega(z_{1},z_{2},{h_{1}})\omega\left(z_{1}z_{2}{h_{1}}{z_{2}}^{-1}{z_{1}}^{-1},z_{1},z_{2}\right)}{\omega\left(z_{1},z_{2}{h_{1}}{z_{2}}^{-1},z_{2}\right)}.

(206)

For every element
{h_{i}}\in{C}
, we introduce a unique representative
x_{i}\in G
such that
x_{i}({h_{1}}){{x_{i}}^{-1}}={h_{i}}
. For convenience, we set
x_{1}=1
.

The simple objects in
\mathrm{Rep}(D^{\omega}G)
are labeled by
(C,\mu)
. For every such pair
(C,\mu)
, we define an irreducible representation
(\pi^{C}_{\mu},V^{C}_{\mu})
of
D^{\omega}(G)
, where
V^{C}_{\mu}=\mathbb{C}[C]\otimes V_{\mu}
is the representation space. We denote by
\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{h}
the generator elements of
D^{\omega}G
, and define the representation matrix by

\pi^{C}_{\mu}(\mathrm{A}^{g}\mathrm{B}^{h})\left|{h_{i},v}\right\rangle=\delta_{h,{h_{i}}}\frac{\beta_{{{x_{i}}^{-1}}hx_{i}}(g,x_{i})}{\beta_{{{x_{i}}^{-1}}hx_{i}}(x_{k},\tilde{g})}\left|{h_{k},\mu({{x_{k}}^{-1}}gx_{i})v}\right\rangle,

(207)

where
v\in V_{\mu}
and
x_{k}
is determined by
g({h_{i}}){{g}^{-1}}={h_{k}}
, and
\tilde{g}={{x_{k}}^{-1}}gx_{i}
.
